lead: Open Windows registry hive files in a window and browse their keys and values. Registry Explorer is a free program by Eric Zimmerman.
use_when: You want to look through a registry hive from a case by hand, key by key.
You need to open several hives at the same time and search across them.
You want to read a hive that is locked on a live system.

features.title: Browsing
items: Shows hives as a tree of keys with their values
Opens more than one hive at the same time
Handles locked files, such as hives from a running system

features.title: Searching and marking
items: A search function for keys and values
Bookmarks to jump back to keys you care about; the manual lists them as a topic

features.title: Plugins
items: The project lists plugin support as a feature
Plugins are an extension point you can add to the program

features.title: Transaction logs
items: Registry Explorer and RECmd ship with rla.exe, which other projects name as a way to merge transaction logs into a hive
Merge the logs before you open a hive, so recent changes are not missed

formats: Registry hive files (NTUSER.DAT, SYSTEM, SOFTWARE, SAM, SECURITY and similar)
requirements: Windows with the .NET 10 Desktop runtime or newer. The current download is for .NET 10 only. The project's page says to unzip with 7-Zip or WinRAR and not to run it from Program Files unless you run as administrator. It is free, but it is not open source.

steps.title: Install the runtime
steps.text: Install the .NET 10 Desktop runtime from Microsoft if your computer does not have it. This is a window-based program, so the Desktop runtime is needed.

steps.title: Download and unzip
steps.text: Download RegistryExplorer.zip from Eric Zimmerman's tools page. Unzip it with 7-Zip or WinRAR into a folder such as C:\Tools\RegistryExplorer, not into Program Files.

steps.title: Prepare your hives
steps.text: Copy the hive files out of your evidence image into a case folder. Work on copies. Keep any transaction log files that sit next to the hive.

steps.title: Start the program
steps.text: Run the program from its folder. If a security warning appears, check the digital signature. The project says all its software is signed, and a valid signature from Eric Zimmerman means antivirus alerts are false.

steps.title: Load a hive
steps.text: Use the program's menu to load a hive file from your case folder. The manual has a chapter on loading hives. You can load more than one hive and switch between them.

steps.title: Browse and search
steps.text: Expand keys in the tree and read the values on the right. Use the search to find a key name, a value name or a piece of data. Add a bookmark for each key you want to report.

steps.title: Write down what you found
steps.text: Record the hive name, the full key path, the value and the key's last write time in your notes. The key path and time are what another examiner needs to verify the finding.

cases.title: Checking one specific key
cases.why: When a report or another tool points to a key, you can open the hive and see the key and its neighbours in context.

cases.title: User activity review
cases.why: NTUSER.DAT holds per-user settings and history. Browsing it shows what a user account did.

cases.title: Software and persistence
cases.why: Looking through the SOFTWARE and NTUSER hives shows installed programs and entries that start programs automatically.

cases.title: Comparing hives
cases.why: With several hives open at once you can check the same key in the hive from different dates or machines.

cases.title: Teaching and practice
cases.why: A visual tree helps students learn how the registry is laid out before they move to command-line parsers.

strengths: Several hives can be open at once, with search across them.
Can read locked hive files, according to the project.
Has a command-line sibling, RECmd, for scripted work.
limits: Free but closed source. The source code is not published.
Windows only, and the current build needs .NET 10.
The project page links no tool-specific manual. The well-known manual is a PDF kept on third-party sites, so check its date.
It shows data one key at a time. For a fast report of many artifacts, a command-line tool is quicker.
A hive copied without its transaction logs can be missing recent changes.
Beginners can get lost in a large hive. Start from a known key path.
